question: Which cup has a higher concentration of sugar?
rewritten_background: Passive transport occurs when a substance passes through the cell membrane without needing any energy to pass through, unlike active transport, which depends on cellular energy and transport proteins working against a concentration difference. In passive transport, the usual idea is that particles spread out from a place where there are more of them packed into the same amount of space to a place where there are fewer. Concentration is the number of particles of a substance in a given volume, so the volume matters just as much as the amount of dissolved material when people compare one solution to another. For example, if one person stirs a teaspoon of salt into a cup of water and another person stirs two teaspoons of salt into another cup of water, people often quickly focus on the larger number of teaspoons, but careful comparisons also pay attention to whether both cups actually contain the same amount of water, whether the salt fully dissolves, and whether either cup is warmer and dissolves the crystals faster. If the cups are the same size and each contains the same volume of water, then the second solution will have a higher concentration of salt. In classroom discussions, people sometimes also mention that a heaping spoonful is not always the same as a level spoonful, that large crystals and fine grains dissolve at different apparent speeds, and that a spoon left wet can make sugar or salt clump, even though concentration is still defined by how much substance is present in a given volume once mixed.
rewritten_situation: A man put two cups, cup A and cup B, filled with equal amounts of water on to a table and walked away to go check his mail. The cups were set near the middle of the table rather than near the edge, and each had been filled to the same water line, although cup A was a slightly narrower cup and cup B was a slightly wider one. The water in both cups had been poured only a minute earlier, and there were a few tiny bubbles clinging to the inner sides of the glass. While the man was outside, his son came along, noticed the two cups, and decided to put some sugar in them to make a tasty drink. He used the same kitchen spoon for both cups, but the spoon still had a few damp grains stuck to it from an earlier rinse, and he stirred cup A first with two quick circular motions before moving on. Into cup A, the child poured two spoonfuls of sugar. Into cup B, he poured three spoonfuls of sugar, but he paused between spoonfuls because the sugar container was a little sticky around the lid, and some of the sugar in that cup briefly sat at the bottom before beginning to dissolve. By the time anyone looked back at the table, cup A appeared clearer while cup B still had a few visible crystals near the base, and the room was warm enough that both cups would eventually dissolve more if left alone.
reasoning: Since concentration depends on particles in a given volume, the details about how the sugar actually dissolved matter here. Cup A was stirred right away, so its two spoonfuls were mixed evenly through the water. Cup B had three spoonfuls added, but some of that sugar was still sitting as visible crystals near the bottom, which means it had not fully dissolved into the solution yet. Concentration should be based on the sugar actually dispersed in the water, not undissolved crystals temporarily resting at the base. Also, cup A looked clearer and was mixed earlier, so its dissolved sugar was already distributed throughout the equal amount of water. Because cup B still had undissolved sugar, the amount of sugar currently in solution could be less than in cup A despite the extra spoonful added. Therefore, the cup with the higher concentration of sugar is cup A.

question: Which cell has a larger volume?
rewritten_background: As a cell grows, its volume increases more quickly than its surface area, a geometric limitation that becomes especially important in active tissues and in laboratory cultures where nutrient uptake, gas exchange, and waste removal must all occur across the cell membrane. In basic terms, even if a cell keeps adding cytoplasm and organelles, the outer membrane does not expand its usable exchange capacity at the same pace, so an overly large cell can face transport bottlenecks. If a cell were to become very large, the comparatively smaller surface area would not allow enough nutrients to enter the cell quickly enough to meet the cell’s needs, and wastes might also leave too slowly. This principle is commonly illustrated in textbook figures comparing small cubes and larger cubes, where the larger shape has much more internal space but proportionally less outer area available for exchange. In real cells, researchers often discuss this in connection with diffusion distances, membrane transport proteins, the rate at which glucose and ions move inward, and the rate at which metabolic by-products move outward. However, large cells do have ways of dealing with some size challenges. Big cells, such as some white blood cells, often grow more nuclei so that they can supply enough proteins and RNA for the cell’s requirements, and in some cases the nuclei may vary somewhat in shape, staining intensity, or position within the cytoplasm depending on the cell cycle and metabolic state. Large, metabolically active cells also often have lots of cell protrusions, resulting in many folds throughout the membrane; these folds can make the perimeter look irregular under a microscope, increase membrane complexity, and provide additional sites where transport can occur. These folds increase the surface area available for transport of materials into or out of the cell. Such cell types are found lining your small intestine, where they absorb nutrients from your food through protrusions called microvilli. Microvilli do not necessarily indicate that a cell has greater total volume, but they do make the membrane more elaborate, and under magnification cells with dense protrusions can appear broader, rougher, or more expanded than smoother neighboring cells even when the key issue being discussed is membrane exchange.

Both cells came from the same organism and were placed in the same nutrient medium, maintained at the same temperature, observed with the same microscope, and recorded on the same data sheet, although the technician noted that the cells did not look identical at the membrane. These cells are from the same organism, but are not the same age. Cell X was created two weeks ago, and cell Z was created one month ago. Therefore, cell Z has had two extra weeks of growth compared to cell X. During observation, cell X was described as having a smoother outline and a more compact appearance, while cell Z was noted to show more visible folds and protrusion-like irregularities around the edge, similar to the kinds of membrane elaborations discussed in highly active cells. The medium in the dish was refreshed every 48 hours, the incubator stayed near 37 degrees Celsius, and both cells remained viable throughout the observation period. The lab notes also mention that older cells in this organism can sometimes show more membrane folding, more pronounced staining around internal structures, and in some cases additional nuclear material to support protein production, though both cells were still classified as individual cells from the same source. The Petri dish was labeled with age, observation time, and magnification, and the older cell, Z, had been monitored over a longer interval simply because it had been present in culture longer.
reasoning: Cell volume is tied to how much of the cell is actually occupied by internal material, not just how old the cell is. Even though cell Z is older, the background emphasizes that large cells run into surface-area-to-volume problems and compensate by increasing membrane folds and protrusions. In the situation, cell Z is specifically described as having more visible folds and protrusion-like irregularities, while cell X has a smoother, more compact appearance. Those folds increase surface area for transport and can make a cell look larger without necessarily increasing its internal bulk. Since older cells may devote growth to extra membrane elaboration and support structures rather than a larger solid body, the smoother and more compact cell X would have the larger true volume, whereas Z's extra apparent size is mainly from folded membrane.
